correctness.rationale: Exact i.i.d. exchangeable covariance transfer is derived from the marginal and pair-inclusion probabilities. Its nonnegative two-mode matrix satisfies \(\det(I-T_\eta)=p\eta^2(1-c)[1+(n-1)c]\{4p-2[p+q(1+(n-2)c)]\eta+q(1-c)[1+(n-1)c]\eta^2\}\). A small-step Lyapunov contraction proves stability; the first positive determinant root is sharp, and the quadratic Lyapunov scaling identity excludes reentry after the larger algebraic root. Permutation symmetrization gives the if-and-only-if statement for every deterministic initial vector. The integer product \((B-m)(B-m-1)\ge0\) proves the sharp unique batch-size law. The expected-objective threshold follows from the exact sampled-Hessian second moment. A standalone verifier passed 2241 assertions including exact symbolic factorization and rational enumeration of all masks for three small dimensions. Edge cases of zero or complete pair activation and integral or nonintegral mean batch size were explicitly included. Finite checks corroborate, but do not prove, the infinite-parameter claim.

originality.rationale: The original mathematical content is not the known arbitrary-sampling probability matrix, the known independent Bernoulli special case, or a generic sufficient rate. It is the complete fixed-expected-work optimization of an exact necessary-and-sufficient mean-square stability threshold over all exchangeable random-subset laws, including the unique adjacent-size optimizer, all-pair-inclusion monotonicity and strict gain over independent activation. Primary full-text comparisons support this distinction; priority remains provisional due to one inaccessible close publication and the ordinary limits of retrieval. The original NSync arbitrary-subset synchronous coordinate method (Richtárik–Takáč, first preprint 2013) was independently compared; it supplies algorithmic precedent and sufficient convergence-rate probability design, not the claimed exact optimizer of the necessary-and-sufficient mean-square stability interval.

value.rationale: For the natural resource constraint of a prescribed expected number of simultaneous coordinate updates, the theorem completely solves which exchangeable batch-size distribution maximizes the actual geometric mean-square stability region. The unique adjacent-size policy is constructive and is strictly safer than iid independent activations at identical expected work. A natural near-rank-one family exhibits a sharp gain approaching a factor of two. The strict gap between one-step expected descent and true asymptotic stability distinguishes rate calibration from monotone surrogate design. The conclusion is neither merely a known sufficient step bound nor an arbitrary unmotivated parameter slice; it solves a complete optimization question over a broad sampling class. No claim of best convergence rate or practical throughput is made.
